rv.q: If this is a jukebox musical, this is how you do it right.
This old-fashioned musical comedy has all the right ingredients — a witty book, gorgeous Gershwin songs and a company of Broadway pros who know how to put over both the jokes and the melodies.
Watching an irresistible force meet an agreeably movable object.
The results are diverting, even if they don't quite match the effervescence of that last excursion.
An alternative title for “Nice Work” might be “It Lukewarm.”
The newly manufactured 1920s-set musical 'Nice Work if You It' crams vintage Gershwin songs into a bubbly crowdpleaser, enchantingly rendered by thesps Kelli O'Hara, Michael McGrath and Judy Kaye.
The show is likable enough, but it feels like a missed opportunity — a chance to create a smart, sophisticated musical comedy that instead settles for adequate.
Overall, the show is too afraid of emotional engagement, which is silly when you have these songs and O'Hara's voice and Broderick's likable self to deliver them.

Who says they don't write Broadway musicals like they used to? Joe DiPietro and Kathleen Marshall have teamed up to reshuffle the Gershwin playlist into a new musical, named for the familiar tune "Nice Work If You It," that is quite simply, to borrow another song title, "Delishious.

The cast is spot-on. Is there any ingenue role in musical theater that Kelli O’Hara — of “The Pajama Game” and “South Pacific” revivals — couldn’t make her very own? In “Nice Work,” even given a stellar cast, when she’s on the stage she often is the single focus, by sheer force of her ability to sing any song fully in character, and deliver it w...
The musical flits between delightful and exasperating on a second-by-second basis.

While Kathleen Marshall's crowd-pleasing production lacks the inspired showstopper choreography of her revival of "Anything Goes," it makes for nonstop giddy fun thanks to its dynamic cast, Joe DiPietro's wickedly funny dialogue and a treasure trove of timeless Gershwin favorites and rarities.

True, Nice Work If You It (* * * out of four) doesn't use an inane story line to simply string together a beloved band or singer's catalog or a bunch of disparate rock chestnuts. Instead, it uses an inane story line to string together the timeless songs of George and Ira Gershwin.
The musical has lovely Gershwin songs and Matthew Broderick's easygoing charm, but the book feels old-fashioned even by Broadway standards.
Unfortunately, 'Nice Work If You It,' despite a few bright spots, fails to hold together as a glittering entertainment.
The result is mostly a flop-sweat inducing affair.
But Marshall hamstrings them all, with arid staging, flaccid pacing, and witless choreography that makes even the peppiest numbers feel leaden.
The show is a perfectly pleasant throwback to the kind of musical theater that Broadway used to do routinely — but it's also the kind of show that makes you realize why Broadway had to evolve.
If only the story hadn’t dragged on and on with multiple endings, “Nice Work” would have made for a nicer evening, away from work.
